read_from: The route text as served: field 1 (the route text) of each row of reader/data/route-store of the main branch at commit 306f3b285898, store_version 87b13b1169b4 (its index.json), for "STEP Bible Translators Amalgamated Hebrew OT aligned component translation" (M4): 95,089 routes (axis: routes), 46,609 letters keys (axis: keys). The definition field of the same row equals the route text on 95,089 of the routes. The source audit: the lane's copy of STEPBible-Data (commit b86d26cdb1f5, in ledgers/work/ldmprs/source-cache/stepbible-data-2026-07-14/), 4 TAHOT files, 305,652 word rows (axis: source rows). Each of the dictionary store's 64,402 records names one such row, and its text equals that row's translation column on 64,402 of them; its two other text fields are filled on 0 and 0 records. A route comes from that one column, so no test here stands on a guess about a field; the audit is evidence about the source and no part of any test. 69,324 routes are a row's whole translation column under the letters of its Hebrew column, 25,764 are a run of a row's word parts that the store cut at the slash under the letters of those parts (the store flags 0 routes as cut), and 1 join no row. Which case of the ask's second sentence: a route here is one rendering of one word form at its places, so the store already gives each rendering its own route; no route holds a comma or a round bracket, the word or stands between words in none, and the word and stands between words only inside one phrase. The source's own key to its signs is on file: the notes at the head of each TAHOT file say that a forward slash separates the translation to mirror the prefixes, root and suffixes in Hebrew, in the Hebrew's order; that words in angle brackets are in the Hebrew but are best not included in a translation; and that words in square brackets are not in the Hebrew but are implied and are best included in a translation. The same files' tag columns, with the short glosses of the source's own lexicon TBESH (H9008 [?], H9010 [the], H9011 [to], H9012 [emph.?], H9013 [emph.?], H9014 [-]), name what the parts ¿, ! and - alone and the endings -ward and -wards stand on. So the shapes that say what those signs are for, and the shapes of words in the two kinds of bracket, rest on that key. Every other shape that says what a sign is for begins "unverified:": the notes speak of words and not of letters in brackets, and they give no account of the question mark, the exclamation mark on a word, the cut hyphen, the colon, the semicolon, a label in brackets or a bracket left open. The shapes of English spelling (a hyphen between two letters, the apostrophe, the point of obj) say only that.

definitions.terms: In every test a character is one Unicode code point (every route holds only characters of 16 bits). A letter is any character of Unicode category L (JavaScript \p{L}); every letter in a route is one of A to Z or a to z. An uppercase letter is one of A to Z, a lowercase letter one of a to z. No route holds a digit. A space is the character U+0020; it is the only whitespace any route holds. Nothing is trimmed: the text is the whole route text as it stands, which is the field route of a line of the by-source JSONL, what the checker gives the classifier, and never the field def. The text before and the text after the mark are the template's c.before and c.after. What a bracket holds is the template's c.group, the same string for an opener and for its closer: the characters between the pair. An opener that never closes has a c.group of null, and a closer that never opened has an empty one. Directly before and directly after name the one character next to the mark; where the mark stands at that end of the text no character stands there, so a test that asks for a character there fails. A string stands between « and », which are not part of it, and every string and every list minds case and is matched exact to the character, spaces included. Begins with and ends with are about the first or last characters of the thing named, with no word boundary. A run of letters is all the letters next to each other, taken as far as the first character that is not a letter or the end of the text; the run of letters directly before the mark ends at the character directly before the mark, and the run directly after it begins at the character directly after the mark; where that character is not a letter the run is empty. A mark's container is the template's c.container: top, bracket for [ ], angle for < >; a bracket character sits in what encloses it.
definitions.first_match: For each mark the shapes are tried in the order they stand in this file; the first whose test holds names the occurrence, and no later shape is tried for it. Not caught above means that no earlier shape of the same mark took the occurrence; a short test below others relies on them. A shape's container field is not part of its test: a test looks at the container only where its words say so, and the checker compares the field afterwards.
definitions.no_bare_word: A step on the whole text, used by the tests that name it. Start a count at nothing. Read the text from its first character to its last: «[» or «<» adds one to the count; «]» or «>» takes one away; a letter read while the count is nothing means the text holds a bare word, and the step answers no. If the end comes and no letter was read while the count was nothing, the step answers yes: the row has no bare word. The step is only reached by a text whose brackets balance, because the tests for unbalanced texts stand first.
definitions.before_the_opener: A step for a closer: take away from the text before the closer what the bracket holds and the opener itself; the character that then stands last is the character directly before this closer's own opener. Where nothing is left, no character stands there and a test that asks for a letter there fails.

The source's own files carry disambiguated Strong's tags in a column of their own, part by part (on 305,638 of 305,652 source rows, axis: source rows), and the route store dropped them: the store's record keeps only the row of one cited place. The letters key here is a word form or a run of its parts, and its routes are the source's renderings of that form at its places, identical ones collapsed, so keys_with_more_than_one_route_text counts renderings at places, not entries. By the audit, which reads the tags of the part or parts each route covers at every row that gives it, of the 15,964 such keys (axis: keys) 9,049 stand on one tag and 6,915 on two or more, so that the texts come from different words that share the letters (example key על, whose routes stand on 6 tags: H5920H, H5921A, H5922, H5923, H5929, H5954).

branches.question: Some rows have no English outside brackets: <the>. The source's note says words in angle brackets are in the Hebrew but best left out of a translation, and words in square brackets are not in the Hebrew but implied. So such a row may give a translator nothing to print for the word. Should the page print these rows as readings? They print as they do today until you rule. To leave them out the page needs one step of its own, because a declaration cannot leave a row out. This answer holds whatever you answer to the other questions.

options.means: The page prints <the> as one reading, as written, as it does today.
The page prints no pill for these rows, once it has the one step of its own that this answer needs; until then they print as they do today. They stay in the store as they are.
